transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-10 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonas Patel (Redwood SE), Ravi Menon (Redwood Solutions), Carlos Rivera (Nimbus CTO), Leah Kim (Nimbus ML Eng), Amir Ghosh (Nimbus Infra), Priya Desai (Nimbus Security)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro from Redwood side — Maya here on AE, Jonas is our SE who will do the deep bits. How are you doing, Carlos?
[00:08] Carlos Rivera: Good, thanks. Trying to chew through our backlog of infra debt. Appreciate the time.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Same here. High level, we got your note about moving away from the mix of OpenAI hosted plus some in-house vLLM for low-latency endpoints. Wanted to learn a bit about constraints and success criteria.
[00:24] Carlos Rivera: Yeah, so two big drivers: latency for patient-facing summarization calls and cost predictability. We currently fan out — the bulk uses OpenAI GPT for general prompts, but our latency spikes so we use vLLM self-host for certain flows. Maintenance of vLLM is fine but ops burden is growing. Also we need to meet data residency for EU patients.
[00:39] Leah Kim: Another note, our eval suite shows subtle drift in hallucination rates between the hosted model and our trimmed quantized vLLM, so parity matters. If we migrate, we need to reproduce our current evals to ensure model behavior is consistent.
[00:51] Jonas Patel: Got it. Two broad axes then: API/behavior parity and infra/cost. Quick question on current inference stack — are you using Text Generation Inference or vanilla vLLM containers?
[00:58] Amir Ghosh: We're mostly on vLLM, custom container, optimized kernels. Some teams tried TGI but refactor cost was too high.
[01:04] Maya Chen: Cool. On Redwood side we support hosted API with OpenAI-like endpoints, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private VPC/on-prem for strict data controls. For parity we usually do a three-way: run the same prompts on OpenAI, your vLLM, and our proposed Redwood config to compare token-level outputs and scoring.
[01:22] Carlos Rivera: How close is Redwood to OpenAI API semantics? We have tools and function-calling expectations baked in.
[01:28] Jonas Patel: We aim for a high degree of compatibility — request/response shapes very similar, streaming, function-style structured output, and we have a compatibility layer for common OpenAI params. There are edge cases — some function-calling behaviors and temperature sampling defaults can differ, and we call those out in the migration checklist.
[01:42] Leah Kim: Sampling and RNG differences are big for us. We run evals with fixed seeds sometimes — can you replicate exact deterministic outputs?
[01:49] Jonas Patel: Determinism is tricky across runtimes, especially with quantized models or different kernels. We can get close — same top-k/top-p settings and seeds help, but exact byte-for-byte parity is unlikely unless it's the same model binary. We recommend focusing on metric parity (ROUGE, factuality checks) rather than exact tokens.
[02:05] Amir Ghosh: On infra, we're worried about latency tail percentiles. vLLM gives us sub-60ms in some flows. How does Redwood handle KV cache and prefix caching?
[02:14] Jonas Patel: Our runtime has continuous batching with intelligent KV cache management — for session-heavy workloads we keep warm caches and can pin shards. For tight tails we advise Dedicated with reserved GPUs and hot warm-up strategies. We can run a microbenchmark against your 99th percentile SLAs.
[02:30] Maya Chen: Also note our Optimize tooling can recommend quantization and batching settings to hit cost targets while keeping quality within thresholds. That's often handy when folks leave vLLM because they were overprovisioned.
[02:40] Carlos Rivera: Security is priority. We need SOC 2, KMS integration for customer-managed keys, SSO/SAML, and audit logs. Also retention and deletion policies for PHI.
[02:50] Priya Desai: Yep — need articulation of e2e encryption, whether the keys ever touch provider-managed hardware, and for Private deployment options whether we can run an air-gapped package for clinical trials.
[02:59] Jonas Patel: We have SOC 2 type II, KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM options for Private), SSO with SAML/OIDC and RBAC. For Private we can do an on-prem bundle with customer-managed HSMs and can scope air-gapped deployments — that will involve a professional services engagement. We'll share our security pack after the call.
[03:18] Leah Kim: For the eval parity tests, we have three canonical prompt families: summarization, triage classification, and discharge note completion. We can provide those to you. What's the usual runtime configuration you test?
[03:29] Jonas Patel: We'll start with the same model family you use (you mentioned a trimmed Llama2-70b quantized). We'll benchmark across sequence lengths matching your median/95th percentiles, test with and without KV caching, and compare both output metrics and perf metrics. If you allow, we'll also include a higher-performing Redwood-verified variant to show latency/cost tradeoffs.
[03:47] Carlos Rivera: Cost model question: how do hosted vs Dedicated vs Private break down for us? We're interested in predictable unit economics for high volume.
[03:55] Maya Chen: Hosted is simplest billing per token with predictable tiers; Dedicated gives predictable throughput with reserved monthly commits and lower per-token pricing; Private has platform fees and infra costs but gives full control for data residency and network isolation. We can model your monthly QPS into a cost estimate — that's part of the pricing packet I'll share.
[04:12] Amir Ghosh: Does Redwood's Dedicated support autoscaling bursts? During peak appointment windows we'll see spikes 3-4x.
[04:19] Maya Chen: Yes — Dedicated supports configurable autoscale policies and burst capacity. You can set baseline reserved and allow short-duration burst capacity with overage pricing.
[04:27] Leah Kim: A small but important point — our eval harness uses some CUDA-specific primitives; will Redwood's runtime accept model artifacts compiled for vLLM/TGI or do we need to recompile?
[04:36] Jonas Patel: Models often need conversion to Redwood's runtime format — usually a straightforward conversion; we provide tooling and, for large customers, we can do the conversion as part of onboarding. TGI/vLLM-specific optimizations might not port verbatim; we'll highlight differences in the conversion report.
[04:49] Carlos Rivera: What's your approach to model updates and version pinning? We need to freeze behavior for clinical features while allowing non-critical models to upgrade.
[04:56] Jonas Patel: You can pin model versions and create rollout policies (canary, A/B). We also support automatic fallback to a pinned variant if a newer model regresses against your eval sets. We recommend creating a gated rollout with metrics-based gates.
[05:09] Priya Desai: For compliance, do you keep detailed audit trails of prompts and inferred outputs? We need to show access logs for audits but also enforce PII redaction policies.
[05:18] Jonas Patel: We have token-level tracing and per-route logging; retention is configurable per account. For PII, we can integrate a pre-send redaction filter, and in Private deploys you control retention entirely.
[05:28] Maya Chen: Quick note on migration pattern — many customers do a hybrid phase: route non-sensitive traffic to Hosted, keep sensitive flows on Private or Dedicated, and gradually migrate once parity and cost thresholds are validated.
[05:39] Carlos Rivera: That sounds like our preferred path. Timeline-wise we hope to decide vendor by May 15 and start pilot by June 1. Is that realistic?
[05:47] Maya Chen: Totally doable. Jonas, can you commit to the 2-week benchmarking plan?
[05:52] Jonas Patel: Yes, we'll run parity tests and share a report in 5 business days. We'll need the prompt sets and some sample traffic traces.
[05:59] Leah Kim: We'll get those over — note some prompts contain PHI so we'll redact before sharing or use synthetic patients.
[06:06] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll also send an initial checklist: security pack, migration steps, typical pitfalls we see with vLLM conversions, and pricing scenarios.
[06:15] Carlos Rivera: Any notable feature gaps compared to GenAI providers? For example, we use a lot of function calls + structured JSON outputs.
[06:23] Jonas Patel: We support function-like structured outputs and can stream partial responses. For complex multi-turn tool flows we recommend instrumenting structured response schemas and we'll show demo examples in the technical deep dive.
[06:34] Ravi Menon: Another thing — if you use embeddings heavily, Redwood supports per-embedding region routing and vector-store integrations. Just flag if you need that.
[06:42] Carlos Rivera: We do use embeddings for search, but that's a secondary migration. Focus first on generative endpoints.
[06:48] Priya Desai: Quick legal/procurement note — we need standard DPAs and clarity on data processor/subprocessor lists. Can you surface that?
[06:56] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll include DPA, subprocessor list, and standard security docs with the pack.
[07:03] Jonas Patel: Recap of technical asks: prompt sets, sample traffic (QPS, seq length distribution), desired latency SLOs, and any special kernel optimizations you've done. We'll baseline the 3 scenarios.
[07:15] Carlos Rivera: I'll coordinate with Leah and Amir to send artifacts by EOD tomorrow.
[07:19] Maya Chen: Great. Any final questions?
[07:22] Leah Kim: One last: if we do Private/on-prem, how long is the onboarding? We have a constrained change window in July.
[07:28] Jonas Patel: For Private on-prem air-gapped, typical lead time is 6-10 weeks including security review and packaging. VPC-hosted Private is faster, 2-4 weeks. We'll map timelines in the follow-up.
[07:38] Maya Chen: Okay, let's capture owners and close out. Thanks everyone for the time.
[07:42] Carlos Rivera: Thanks all. Talk soon.
